newsitem.title: CHINA: China soybean import quota seen barrier to WTO.
newsitem.headline: China soybean import quota seen barrier to WTO.

text.p: U.S. soybean farmers are looking forward to the day China lifts quota requirements on imports of soybeans and soybean products and allows them to be freely traded, U.S. industry representatives said on Tuesday.
Such quotas were a major sticking point in China's application to join the World Trade Organisation (WTO), said Robert Williams, a trade analyst with the United Soybean Board (USB).
"We would like to see the Chinese government move towards freer trade," Williams told Reuters.

China currently sets a limit, which it does not make public, on imports of soybeans and soybean oil. Soybeans imported within the limit are subject to three percent import duty, plus a value-added tax (VAT) of 13 percent.
Soybeans imported outside the quota are subject to import tax of 114 percent, though Williams said he did not know of any imports having been subject to that rate.
Soybean oil imported within the quota is subject to 13 percent import duty, which rises to 118 percent if it is imported outside the quota limits, he said.
Soybean meal imports were liberalised in 1996, and carry no VAT.
Williams was attending a conference on China's vegetable oils, fats and feed ingredients industries.

The conference, organised by Singapore's Centre for Management Technology, heard from a representative of China's major food trading arm National Cereals, Oils and Foodstuffs Import and Export Corporation (COFCO), that the quota system aims to maintain market stability.

The head of COFCO's import division, Bian Jun, said the import licensing system for vegetable oil could be readjusted according to domestic demand. He gave no further details, but said six Chinese companies, including COFCO, are currently permitted to import vegetable oil. Joint venture companies can import freely but only for their own needs, he said.
Williams said the USB, which is funded by U.S. soybean farmers, supported China's bid to join the WTO.
Membership would give the world's biggest importer of soybean products a position in world trade "via fairer and easier trade between countries", he said.
"It will also give them an avenue for settling disputes that they don't have today," he said.
Williams said he would be meeting with Chinese government officials while in Beijing to call for greater transparency in China's production and consumption of soybeans and soybean products.
"We would like to know those needs, we would like to provide for those needs and also to know how our farmers in the U.S. can provide for those needs with production," he said.
By 2005, China's annual imports of soybeans should reach 12 million tonnes, from projected imports for the current (Sept 1-Aug 30) marketing year of 2.5 million tonnes, he said.
Imports to date this marketing year are 1.5 million tonnes, 90 percent from the United States, Williams said.
The United States expected to have 80 percent of China's soybean imports for the total 1996/97 marketing year, he said.
China also imports South American soybeans.
